paragraphs: Before the next review, members checked whether the posted explanation could be understood without attending the original meeting. A student who had been absent could find the winning proposal, but could not see why a cheaper alternative had been rejected. The council added a short comparison showing how both ideas met the published criteria. Listing the rules was not the same as showing how they had been applied to a particular choice.

Another reader noticed that an estimated cost had been copied incorrectly. Members corrected the figure and kept a note of the correction beside the explanation. They did not describe the earlier mistake as evidence that openness had failed. Making the reasoning visible had allowed someone else to question a detail that mattered. The next budget review would still involve difficult choices and incomplete information. However, students now had a clearer way to distinguish disagreement about priorities from an error in the facts. The council treated transparency as a practice of explaining and correcting, rather than a claim that publishing one notice made every decision beyond criticism.
rationale: transparentを意思決定の基準・適用・訂正可能性から読む。関係節、受動態、形式目的語、動名詞と完了形を扱う。

paragraphs: For the next class project, students made a small table showing the purpose of each reserved period. Testing time included watching a new visitor use a display and leaving room to act on what was observed. A trial at the very last minute would reveal problems without giving anyone a chance to repair them. The class therefore placed a short correction period after the trial, rather than treating the trial itself as the final task.

When one model took longer to build than expected, members discussed which features could be simplified. They did not quietly borrow all the testing time to finish an extra moving part. The table made the cost of that choice visible: more building would mean less opportunity to check whether people understood the result. Allocating time did not make delays disappear or give the class more afternoons. It made competing uses of the same hours easier to compare. At the final project review, students carefully considered both what they had built and whether the protected periods had served their intended purposes.
rationale: allocateを有限時間の優先事項と機会費用から読む。関係節、間接疑問、否定、動名詞と不定詞の働きを扱う。

paragraphs: During the trial, one night worker reported that noise continued after the agreed time on two days. The mediator asked residents to discuss those occasions rather than return immediately to the claim that one group should lose all use of the courtyard. Families explained that the posted hours were difficult to read from the play area. The group then moved the shared notice and agreed who would remind visitors of the shared conditions.

At the review date, residents considered both the location of activities and the way the agreement had been explained. They kept the smaller play area but adjusted one period after hearing from people who had not attended the first meeting. The change did not prove that the original compromise had been pointless. A trial had provided evidence about how the plan worked in daily life. Important interests could remain stable even when the practical arrangement needed revision. Compromise meant continuing to make room for those interests, not demanding that people stop reporting problems once they had accepted an initial plan.
rationale: compromiseを重要な利害の保護と取決めの修正から読む。関係節、間接疑問、完了形、譲歩と限定を扱う。

paragraphs: The instructor later asked her to keep both versions and record exactly which colors she had changed. Remembering that one picture felt warmer was not enough to explain the decision to another painter. A short note beside the images helped her return to the same relationship instead of searching through the whole painting again.

She also noticed that the classroom light changed how the shadows appeared. For a later comparison, she showed the two versions in the same place under the same light. This did not turn the exercise into a perfect scientific test, but reduced one source of confusion. She asked viewers to describe what they saw before offering her own interpretation.

Some noticed the warmer shadow immediately; others continued to focus on the flowers. Their different reactions did not make the change meaningless or prove that everyone experienced it in the same way. The student learned to distinguish the small choice she had made from the range of responses it could invite. A subtle effect could matter without being equally obvious to every viewer.
rationale: subtleを小さいが意味を持つ色差と観客の多様な反応から読む。分詞、知覚構文、間接疑問と比較条件の限定を扱う。

paragraphs: Before another demonstration, the club wrote the agreed steps on a shared sheet. It included a place to record interruptions or mistakes rather than quietly repeating a trial until the result looked attractive. If a group could not follow a step, its record would say what had happened. Keeping the procedure consistent did not mean pretending that every attempt had gone exactly as planned. Readers needed to know where the intended method and the actual work differed.

Students then compared notes from more than one trial for each filter. Results could vary even when the main conditions were kept the same. They described that variation instead of selecting only the clearest sample. A difference seen once might need further investigation before it could support a strong conclusion about a material. The report kept its narrow purpose: a classroom comparison of visible changes under stated conditions. It did not claim to establish which water was safe to drink. A consistent method made the evidence easier to examine, while an honest record showed how far that evidence could reasonably be used.
rationale: consistentを手順の安定と結果の変動の区別から読む。受動態、間接疑問、関係節、完了形と否定を扱う。
